result.summary: The Chorus of Ocean's daughters shudders at Io's fate and prays never to wed a god. Prometheus boasts that Zeus will fall through a marriage, and defies Hermes, who demands the secret and threatens worse torment. Prometheus refuses, the Chorus stays loyal, and Zeus's storm engulfs them all.

scenes.title: The Chorus Fears Divine Marriage
scenes.summary: The Chorus prays never to marry a god, fearing Io's fate. Prometheus predicts that Zeus will be overthrown through a marriage and that only he knows how to prevent it.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus risks further punishment by openly prophesying and cursing the downfall of Zeus.

place.name: The rock in the Scythian wilds

scenes.title: Prometheus Defies the Chorus
scenes.summary: In short exchanges Prometheus says he fears nothing since he cannot die, and scorns Zeus and Necessity.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus faces harsher torment from Zeus but says he is prepared for it.

place.name: The rock in the Scythian wilds

scenes.title: Hermes Demands the Secret
scenes.summary: Hermes arrives and demands the details of the marriage that will unseat Zeus. Prometheus refuses, and Hermes threatens burial in the rock and the eagle tearing his liver.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus faces burial under the shattered cliff and the eagle's daily feeding on his liver.

place.name: The rock in the Scythian wilds

scenes.title: The Storm Swallows Prometheus
scenes.summary: The Chorus refuses to abandon Prometheus despite Hermes's warning. Zeus's storm breaks and Prometheus, calling on the firmament, vanishes with the Chorus.
scenes.stakes: The Chorus and Prometheus are overwhelmed by Zeus's thunder and earthquake.

place.name: The rock in the Scythian wilds

alias_notes.explanation: Hermes calls Zeus the Father, as father of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Prometheus's defiant claim of immortality, showing his fearlessness.
Concise statement of his contempt for Zeus.
Hermes's sharp retort that Zeus never says 'alas'.

analysis.text: The scene contrasts tyranny and defiance: Zeus's power rests on force, while Prometheus's knowledge and endurance give him moral strength.
The Chorus's praise of marrying within one's rank reflects Greek social attitudes about marriage and status.

legacy.text: The image of the eagle feeding on Prometheus's liver became the standard emblem of the myth in later art and literature.

fun_facts.text: The play's ending, with Prometheus engulfed by the storm, was probably staged with stage machinery, as the chorus and hero 'disappear'.

language_notes.text: "In sooth" means truly; "in one's own degree" means within one's own social rank. The chorus endorses marrying an equal.
The Fates were goddesses who governed destiny, so the chorus appeals to them to prevent a marriage with Zeus.
"A war against which there is no warring" means a conflict that cannot be resisted; "resourceless" means offering no way out.
"Malison" means a curse; "imprecated" means called down. Cronus cursed his son Zeus when Zeus overthrew him.
"Levin" is an archaic word for lightning; "in his own despite" means through his own doing, against his own interest.
"Sooth" means truly or in truth; "imprecate" means to call down curses. The Chorus says Prometheus is merely wishing harm on Zeus.
"Bear upon his neck" pictures a yoke; Zeus will carry pangs as a beast carries its burden. "Galling" means chafing and painful.
"For aught I care" means "I do not care at all what he does."
Necessity (Ananke) was the impersonal power of fate to which even gods were thought subject. The bracketed [13] is the translator's footnote marker.
"His little day" means Zeus's brief time of rule; "bear sway" means to rule.
"Lackey" and "servitor" both mean a servant; Prometheus uses them contemptuously for Hermes, the messenger of Zeus.
"Harbinger" means to announce or herald something; "hath" is the archaic form of "has".
"Creatures of a day" means mortals, whose lives are brief. Prometheus's crime was giving them honours and fire.
"Double journey" means Hermes does not want to be sent back a second time because Prometheus gave an evasive answer.
"Minion" here means a servile underling or favourite, and is meant as an insult.
The two earlier sovereigns are Uranus and Cronus, who were overthrown before Zeus took power.
"Scurry" mocks Hermes as a hurrying servant; "naught" means nothing.
Hermes answers with sarcasm: it is "better" to serve the rock, he says, meaning Prometheus has made a foolish choice.
Prometheus says he would not have spoken so to Hermes, a mere servant, if he had learned sobriety; he is mockingly insulting him as an underling.
Sarcasm: Prometheus says he owes Zeus a debt of gratitude, meaning he owes him nothing.
"Girdest at me" means jeer or mock; "forsooth" means indeed, used sarcastically.
"Levin" is an archaic word for lightning, here Zeus's thunderbolt.
Prometheus scorns the idea of acting "womanish" and begging with upturned hands; this reflects the ancient Greek gender attitudes of the play.
Horse-taming imagery: a colt that takes the bit between its teeth escapes control. Hermes uses it to describe Prometheus's obstinacy.
"Banqueter" here means the eagle as an uninvited diner; "rents" are tears or gashes.
Alludes to a god taking Prometheus's suffering on himself and descending to Tartarus; the myth is usually read as the centaur Chiron, who gave up his immortality.
"Sooth" means truth; "vaunting" means boasting.
"Seemeth" and "bids" are archaic forms; "untimely" here means unreasonably or inappropriately.
Tartarus is the deepest abyss of the underworld, where Zeus imprisoned his enemies, the Titans among them.
"Stern Necessity" refers to Fate, the power to which even Zeus is said to be subject in this play.
"Withdraw amain" means depart at once, with full force; "compassionate" is used as a verb meaning pity.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe"; "strain" means manner of speech.
"Toils" means a hunter's net or snares; "unawares" means by surprise.
"Holy mother" is Themis (also called Earth), Prometheus's mother in this play; he appeals to her and the sky.

context_notes.text: Io was a maiden loved by Zeus and turned into a cow. Hera, his jealous wife, tormented her with a gadfly that drove her across the world.
Prometheus alone knows a secret about the marriage that will topple Zeus. This gives him leverage against his tormentor.
Poseidon, Zeus's brother, ruled the sea and earthquakes. His trident is his weapon.
Prometheus is an immortal Titan, so Zeus can torment him but cannot kill him. This is why he claims to be beyond fear.
Prometheus knows a secret about a marriage that will lead to Zeus's downfall. This is why he confidently predicts Zeus will not reign long.
Hermes is the messenger god, sent by Zeus (the "Father") to force Prometheus to reveal the prophecy about Zeus's downfall.
Prometheus knows a secret about a marriage that would produce a son mightier than his father, and Zeus wants to learn whom to avoid.
"The Father" is Zeus, king of the gods. Hermes is his messenger and servant.
Zeus's threat is to bury Prometheus under the broken cliff, so the punishment is renewed rather than ended.
In the myth, Zeus's eagle eats Prometheus's liver, which regrows each day, making the torment endless.
Hermes is Zeus's messenger, sent to force Prometheus to reveal the secret of which marriage will threaten Zeus's rule.
The Chorus are the daughters of Oceanus, sympathetic sea nymphs who have stayed to comfort Prometheus.

literary_notes.text: "A war against which there is no warring" is a paradoxical phrase that conveys the helplessness of mortals before the gods.
Prometheus mocks Zeus's confidence in his thunder and bolt, which he says cannot save him. This ironic taunt builds on the coming reversal.
The contrast of sovereign and slave closes the scene. It points at Prometheus's own bondage and hints at Zeus's future fall.
Prometheus answers fear with a question, making his fearlessness seem obvious and turning the Chorus's challenge back on them.
His commands to "worship, adore, and fawn" are bitterly sarcastic, mocking the Chorus's servility and, by extension, those who flatter tyrants.
Caring "less than naught" exaggerates his contempt to show total defiance of Zeus.
Prometheus paints the new gods as young, arrogant and complacent, and sets his own long memory against their false security.
Prometheus prophesies that Zeus will fall as his predecessors did, which anticipates the play's central conflict.
Prometheus, chained and in agony, claims his lot is preferable to Hermes's comfortable service, reversing the apparent power between them.
Prometheus throws Hermes's word "revel" back at him, turning the taunt into a curse on his enemies.
Hermes calls "Alas" unknown to Zeus, implying Zeus never suffers. Prometheus counters that time teaches everything, hinting at Zeus's eventual fall.
Prometheus compares Hermes's persuasion to pleading with a wave, an image of his unyielding, rock-like resistance.
Prometheus is likened to a new-harnessed colt fighting the reins, showing his stubbornness through an image of an untamed animal.
Suffering is imagined as a tempest and towering wave breaking over Prometheus, making the coming punishment vivid and overwhelming.
Hermes says Zeus never lies. This portrays Zeus as a ruler whose threats are certain, and Hermes as his loyal spokesman.
Prometheus piles up cosmic catastrophes, inviting the whole universe to be overturned, to show that nothing can break his will.
Hermes calls Prometheus mad, yet the defiance he mocks proves a steadfast resolve, which the play presents as heroic.
The Chorus's loyalty and hatred of traitors contrasts with Hermes, who serves Zeus obediently.
Vivid sound and sight imagery of quake, thunder, lightning and winds makes the storm overwhelming, as the earth and sky merge in chaos.
Prometheus addresses the firmament as witness, appealing to nature as the only audience left to his suffering.
